claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles possess high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy raises atomic diffusion barriers in the nanoparticles.
Entropy-induced diffusion barriers inhibit nanoparticle sintering at elevated temperature.
Entropy-induced diffusion barriers inhibit chemical segregation at elevated temperature.
Defect-engineered supports form strong interfacial bonds with the nanoparticles.
Defect-mediated interfacial bonding provides robust anchoring points for the nanoparticles.
Robust anchoring by support defects further suppresses nanoparticle sintering.
Robust anchoring by support defects preserves nanoparticle chemical homogeneity.
Nanoparticles on defect-engineered supports will show less sintering and aggregation than otherwise identical nanoparticles on inert supports.
Nanoparticles on defect-engineered supports will show less compositional segregation than those on inert supports.
Nanoparticles on inert supports will undergo greater coalescence because elevated temperature permits unmitigated surface diffusion.
Nanoparticles on inert supports will develop greater chemical inhomogeneity than those on defect-engineered supports.
The stabilization effect requires a support-defect density sufficient to overcome thermal effects in the stated temperature ranges.
The stabilization mechanism may cease to apply when alloy composition deviates markedly from near-equiatomic ratios.
The proposed stabilization may fail in reactive oxidizing environments.
Oxidation can produce composition inversion and chemically layered surface oxides in an equiatomic complex alloy.
The initial nanoparticles have a uniform distribution of constituent elements and low noble-metal content.
Holding nanoparticle composition and noble-metal content constant while changing only the support is intended to isolate the support-defect effect.
Particle size, aggregation state, and compositional homogeneity can be compared over time using TEM and EDS mapping.
Similar sintering, aggregation, and chemical inhomogeneity on engineered and inert supports would falsify the claimed stabilizing effect of defect-mediated support interactions.
